paragraphs: The power to regulate the militia and to command its services in times of insurrection and invasion comes naturally with the duties of overseeing the common defense and watching over the internal peace of the Confederacy.

It takes no skill in the science of war to see that uniformity in the organization and discipline of the militia would have the most beneficial effects whenever they were called into service for the public defense. It would enable them to carry out the duties of the camp and the field with mutual understanding and coordination, an advantage of particular importance in the operations of an army. It would also fit them to reach much sooner the degree of proficiency in military functions that is essential to their usefulness. This desirable uniformity can be achieved only by entrusting the regulation of the militia to the direction of the national authority. It is, therefore, with the most evident propriety that the plan of the Convention proposes to empower the Union "to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia, and for governing such part of them as may be employed in the service of the United States, RESERVING TO THE STATES RESPECTIVELY THE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS, AND THE AUTHORITY OF TRAINING THE MILITIA ACCORDING TO THE DISCIPLINE PRESCRIBED BY CONGRESS."

Of all the grounds taken against the plan of the Convention, none was so little to be expected, or is so indefensible in itself, as the one from which this particular provision has been attacked. If a well-regulated militia is the most natural defense of a free country, it ought certainly to be under the regulation and at the disposal of the body that has been made the guardian of the national security. If standing armies are dangerous to liberty, then an effective power over the militia, held by the body charged with protecting the State, ought as far as possible to remove the inducement and the pretext for such unfriendly institutions. If the federal government can command the help of the militia in those emergencies that call for the military arm in support of the civil authority, it can the better do without a different kind of force. If it cannot make use of the former, it will be obliged to turn to the latter. Making an army unnecessary will be a surer way of preventing its existence than a thousand prohibitions on paper.

To cast odium on the power of calling out the militia to execute the laws of the Union, it has been remarked that the proposed Constitution nowhere provides for calling out the POSSE COMITATUS to assist the public officer in the performance of his duty. From this it has been inferred that military force was intended to be his only auxiliary. There is a striking incoherence in the objections that have appeared, sometimes even from the same quarter, and it is not much calculated to inspire a very favorable opinion of the sincerity or fair dealing of their authors. The same persons who tell us in one breath that the powers of the federal government will be despotic and unlimited inform us in the next that it does not have authority enough even to call out the POSSE COMITATUS. The latter, fortunately, falls as far short of the truth as the former exceeds it. It would be as absurd to doubt that a right to pass all laws NECESSARY AND PROPER to execute its declared powers would include the right to require the assistance of the citizens to the officers entrusted with executing those laws, as it would be to believe that a right to enact laws necessary and proper for imposing and collecting taxes would include the right to change the rules of inheritance and of the transfer of landed property, or to abolish trial by jury in cases relating to it. It is therefore evident that the supposition that the government lacks power to require the aid of the POSSE COMITATUS is entirely without foundation. It follows that the conclusion drawn from it, as applied to the authority of the federal government over the militia, is as unfair as it is illogical. What reason could there be to infer that force was intended to be the sole instrument of authority, merely because there is a power to use it when necessary? What shall we think of the motives that could induce men of sense to reason in this manner? How shall we prevent a conflict between charity and conviction?

By a curious refinement on the spirit of republican jealousy, we are even taught to fear danger from the militia itself in the hands of the federal government. It is observed that select corps may be formed, made up of the young and ardent, who may be made subservient to the aims of arbitrary power. What plan for regulating the militia the national government may follow is impossible to foresee. But I am so far from viewing the matter as those who object to select corps as dangerous do that, if the Constitution were ratified and I were to give my views on a militia establishment to a member of the federal legislature from this State, I should put to him, in substance, the following discourse:

"The project of disciplining all the militia of the United States would be as futile as it would be harmful, if it could be carried out. A tolerable skill in military movements is a matter that takes time and practice. A day, or even a week, will not suffice to attain it. To require the great body of the yeomanry and of the other classes of citizens to be under arms for military exercises and maneuvers as often as might be needed to reach the degree of perfection that would entitle them to be called a well-regulated militia would be a real grievance to the people and a serious public problem and loss. It would take an annual deduction from the productive labor of the country that, calculated on the present numbers of the people, would not fall far short of the whole expense of the civil establishments of all the States. To attempt something that would cut down the mass of labor and industry to so considerable an extent would be unwise, and the experiment, if made, could not succeed, because it would not long be endured. Little more can reasonably be aimed at, with respect to the people at large, than to have them properly armed and equipped; and to see that this is not neglected, it will be necessary to assemble them once or twice in the course of a year.

"But though the scheme of disciplining the whole nation must be given up as harmful or impracticable, it is extremely important that a well-considered plan be adopted as soon as possible for properly establishing the militia. The government should give its attention especially to forming a select corps of moderate size, on principles that will truly fit its members for service in case of need. By limiting the plan in this way, we can have an excellent body of well-trained militia ready to take the field whenever the defense of the State requires it. This will not only lessen the call for military establishments. It also means that if circumstances should ever oblige the government to form an army of any size, that army can never be a threat to the liberties of the people, so long as there is a large body of citizens, little if at all inferior to the army in discipline and the use of arms, who stand ready to defend their own rights and those of their fellow-citizens. This seems to me the only substitute that can be devised for a standing army, and the best possible security against one, should it come into existence."

Thus I should reason on the same subject very differently from the adversaries of the proposed Constitution, drawing arguments for safety from the very sources they represent as full of danger and ruin. But how the national legislature may reason on the point is something that neither they nor I can foresee.

There is something so far-fetched and extravagant in the idea of danger to liberty from the militia that one is at a loss whether to treat it gravely or with mockery: whether to consider it a mere display of skill, like the paradoxes of rhetoricians; a dishonest trick to plant prejudices at any price; or the serious offspring of political fanaticism. Where, in the name of common sense, are our fears to end if we may not trust our sons, our brothers, our neighbors, our fellow-citizens? What shadow of danger can there be from men who mingle every day with the rest of their countrymen and share with them the same feelings, views, habits and interests? What reasonable cause for fear can be drawn from a power in the Union to prescribe regulations for the militia and to command its services when necessary, while the individual States are to have the SOLE AND EXCLUSIVE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS? If it were possible to entertain seriously a jealousy of the militia under any conceivable establishment by the federal government, the fact that the officers are appointed by the States ought at once to put an end to it. There can be no doubt that this fact will always secure the States a preponderating influence over the militia.

In reading many of the publications against the Constitution, a man is likely to imagine that he is reading some badly written tale or romance. Instead of natural and pleasing images, it shows the mind nothing but frightful and distorted shapes—
discoloring and disfiguring whatever it represents, and turning everything it touches into a monster.

A sample of this appears in the exaggerated and improbable claims that have been made about the power of calling for the militia's services. The New Hampshire militia, we are told, is to be marched to Georgia, Georgia's to New Hampshire, New York's to Kentucky, and Kentucky's to Lake Champlain. Indeed, the debts owed to the French and Dutch are to be paid in militiamen instead of louis d'ors and ducats. At one moment there is to be a large army to crush the liberties of the people. At another, the militia of Virginia are to be dragged five or six hundred miles from their homes to tame the republican stubbornness of Massachusetts, while Massachusetts's militia are to be carried the same distance to subdue the unruly haughtiness of the aristocratic Virginians. Do the people who rave in this fashion imagine that their art or eloquence can make the people of America accept any fancy or absurdity as infallible truth?

If there should be an army to use as the engine of despotism, what need is there of the militia? If there should be no army, where would the militia go, irritated at being called on to undertake a distant and hopeless expedition to rivet the chains of slavery on a part of their countrymen? Would they not head straight for the seat of the tyrants who had planned so foolish as well as so wicked a project, to crush them in their imagined entrenchments of power and to make them an example of the just vengeance of an abused and enraged people? Is this the way usurpers stride to dominion over a numerous and enlightened nation? Do they begin by arousing the detestation of the very instruments of their intended usurpations? Do they usually begin their career with wanton and disgusting acts of power, calculated to serve no end but to draw universal hatred and execration on themselves? Are suppositions of this sort the sober warnings of discerning patriots to a discerning people? Or are they the inflammatory ravings of incendiaries or deranged enthusiasts? Even if we were to suppose the national rulers driven by the most ungovernable ambition, it is impossible to believe that they would use such preposterous means to accomplish their designs.

In times of insurrection or invasion, it would be natural and proper for the militia of a neighboring State to be marched into another to resist a common enemy, or to guard the republic against the violence of faction or sedition. This was frequently done, as to the first object, in the course of the recent war, and this mutual help is indeed a principal end of our political association. If the power of giving it is placed under the direction of the Union, there will be no danger of a sluggish and listless inattention to the dangers of a neighbor until its near approach had added the urgings of self-preservation to the too feeble impulses of duty and sympathy.
